title: Continuous Pretraining
blurb: Tests what continuous pretraining changes compared with fine-tuning and RAG, when a domain gap is real, catastrophic forgetting and data mixing, the 6ND compute rule and 16 bytes per parameter, LoRA's memory saving, the curation pipeline, and why legal text surprised GPT-2.

questions.prompt: What does continuous pretraining change, in the chapter's terms?
options: How the model behaves, such as the format and tone of its answers
What the model can look up at inference time, without touching the weights
What the model knows, by putting domain knowledge into the weights
Which tokens the model's vocabulary contains, by retraining the tokenizer from scratch
questions.explanation: CPT teaches the model what to know. Behaviour and tone are instruction fine-tuning's job. Looking up facts at inference time without changing weights is RAG. CPT keeps the tokenizer and continues next-token training.

questions.prompt: What training objective does CPT use?
options: Reinforcement learning from human preferences over pairs of answers
Contrastive learning that pulls similar sentence embeddings together
Supervised learning on instruction and response pairs written by experts
Next-token prediction on domain text, as in pretraining
questions.explanation: CPT keeps the pretraining objective and changes the data. It is self-supervised, so it needs no labels. Instruction pairs are IFT, and preference learning is RLHF.

questions.prompt: Why does continued next-token training on domain text teach domain knowledge?
options: Each domain document is stored in the weights word for word, ready to be recalled on request.
The training labels mark which facts are important for the model to learn.
Predicting domain text well forces it to learn the domain's words and conventions.
Next-token prediction adds new layers for each domain the model sees.
questions.explanation: To predict domain text, the model has to build representations of its syntax, semantics and conventions. There are no labels, and no layers are added. Storing text verbatim is memorisation, which the chapter treats as a risk.

questions.prompt: Procedure 33.1 divides domain perplexity by general perplexity. What does a ratio below 1.2 mean?
options: The model has already been through CPT on this exact domain at some earlier point in its life.
The base model handles the domain well enough, so CPT is unlikely to be worth it.
The domain text is too short for perplexity to be measured reliably.
There is a large domain gap, so CPT is likely to pay off.
questions.explanation: The listing's comments give the thresholds: below 1.2, the base model copes. Above 2.0, there is a large gap and CPT is likely valuable.

questions.prompt: Which domain features does the chapter say make CPT worth considering? Select all that apply.
options: Knowledge that postdates the model's training cutoff
Novel notation, such as legal citations or a proprietary code dialect
A domain that feels specialised, whatever a perplexity test shows
Specialised words whose meaning differs from everyday use
questions.explanation: The chapter lists specialised vocabulary, novel notation, domain reasoning patterns and post-cutoff knowledge. It insists the decision rest on a measured perplexity test, not on how specialised a domain feels.

questions.prompt: A team wants to run CPT on standard Python code. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Run it. Code is always poorly covered by web text, so the gain from CPT will be large.
Run it, but only with LoRA, since full CPT can't learn programming languages.
Skip any test. Code domains always give a perplexity ratio above 2.0.
It's rarely worth it. Python is well represented already, so prompting or IFT is cheaper.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives standard Python as an example of a well-represented domain, where CPT rarely pays. A perplexity test would show it. Nothing says code domains always have large gaps.

questions.prompt: What is catastrophic forgetting in CPT?
options: General abilities degrade as training pushes hard toward the new domain.
The model forgets the domain text once training ends and the weights are saved.
The tokenizer drops rare words it hasn't seen in the domain corpus.
Training stops early because the loss stops falling after the first epoch.
questions.explanation: Gradients optimise for the new distribution and can erode what the model knew before. That is the central risk of CPT. It has nothing to do with saving weights or the tokenizer.

questions.prompt: What is the standard data-mixing mitigation, and the usual starting ratio?
options: Train on general text only for the first half of the run, then switch to domain text.
Blend in general text from the original distribution, often 80–90% domain to 10–20% general.
Use domain text only, but repeat each document many times so the model holds on to the general skills.
Mix 50% domain text with 50% instruction pairs to keep the model helpful.
questions.explanation: Mixing in 10–20% general text keeps the old distribution in view. The chapter says the right ratio depends on the domain and needs testing. Repeating documents encourages memorisation.

questions.prompt: Besides data mixing, which mitigations for forgetting does the chapter list? Select all that apply.
options: Replay buffers that re-include original-distribution examples
A learning rate 10 to 100 times lower than original pretraining
A learning rate 10 times higher, so the domain is learned before forgetting starts
Running CPT through LoRA adapters so fewer parameters can drift
questions.explanation: Lower learning rates, replay buffers and LoRA all limit how far the weights move from where they were. A higher learning rate would make forgetting worse.

questions.prompt: In C ≈ 6ND, where does the 6 come from?
options: About 2 FLOPs per parameter per token in the forward pass and 4 in the backward pass
Six epochs, the usual number of passes over a CPT corpus
Six GPUs, the usual size of a training node
Six bytes per parameter for weights, gradients and optimiser state, summed over a step
questions.explanation: Forward costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, and backward about twice that. N is parameters and D is training tokens. Memory per parameter is a separate figure, 16 bytes for mixed-precision Adam.

questions.prompt: Using C ≈ 6ND, how many FLOPs does CPT of a 7-billion-parameter model on 1 billion tokens take? Give the answer in units of 10^19.
That 4.2 × 10^19 FLOP run uses one GPU with a 312 TFLOPS peak at 40% utilisation, as in Listing 33.2. How many GPU-hours does it take? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Achieved rate = 312 × 10^12 × 0.4 = 1.248 × 10^14 FLOP/s. Time = 4.2 × 10^19 / 1.248 × 10^14 = 336,538 s, which is 93.5 hours. Using peak instead would give about 37 hours, the 2–3x underestimate the procedure warns about.

questions.prompt: Mixed-precision Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter. How many GB is that for a full fine-tune of a 7-billion-parameter model, before activations? Use 1 GB = 10^9 bytes.
questions.explanation: 16 × 7 × 10^9 = 112 × 10^9 bytes. That already exceeds one 80 GB GPU, which is why ZeRO, checkpointing or LoRA come in.

questions.prompt: Using Listing 33.2's LoRA rule, memory = 2N + 16 × (N × 0.01), how many GB does the same 7B model need? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 2 × 7 × 10^9 = 14 GB for the frozen bf16 weights, plus 16 × 7 × 10^7 = 1.12 GB for the adapters. The total is 15.12 GB, against 112 GB for the full fine-tune.

questions.prompt: Where do the 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam come from?
options: 2 for bf16 weights and 14 for the KV cache built up during the forward pass
2 for bf16 weights, 2 for bf16 gradients, and 4 each for fp32 master weights and two Adam moments
8 for the weights at double precision, plus 8 for the second copy kept for gradient checkpointing
4 for fp32 weights, 4 for fp32 gradients, and 8 for the activations of one batch
questions.explanation: 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16. The chapter stresses this is before activations are counted, which come on top. The KV cache is an inference-time cost, not a training-state one.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 33.3 say never to skip deduplication?
options: Duplicates improve quality, so the procedure keeps them and removes only short documents.
Duplicates are needed for replay buffers, so removing them causes forgetting later in training.
Duplicates make the model memorise instead of generalise, and waste compute on repeated tokens.
Duplicates make the tokenizer crash on the second copy of any document.
questions.explanation: The procedure's common mistake: duplicates push memorisation and inflate cost for no benefit. The pipeline uses exact hashing plus MinHash LSH for near-duplicates.

questions.prompt: How much domain text does the chapter say CPT needs?
options: Exactly as many tokens as the original pretraining, or forgetting wins
About 1,000 carefully curated examples, as in the LIMA paper
A few hundred documents, since the base model already knows the language
At least 10 million tokens, and preferably over a billion
questions.explanation: The trade-offs section gives 10M+ tokens as the minimum and 1B+ as preferred. Small corpora lead to memorisation. LIMA's 1,000 examples is about instruction fine-tuning, where quality beats quantity.

questions.prompt: A customer wants the model to answer in a strict support-ticket format. Is CPT the right tool?
options: Yes, as long as the corpus has more than 10 million tokens of tickets.
Yes. CPT is the only way to change a model's output format reliably once it is deployed.
No. Formats can only be changed by retraining the model from scratch.
No. That is a behaviour change, which is instruction fine-tuning's job.
questions.explanation: The chapter says CPT breaks down when the need is behavioural, not knowledge. Format and tone are IFT's domain. Corpus size doesn't change which tool fits.

questions.prompt: GPT-2 small scored perplexity 26.53 on legal text and 31.54 on general text. What is the legal/general ratio? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 26.53 / 31.54 = 0.84. That is below 1.2, so by Procedure 33.1 the base model handles this domain well enough.

questions.prompt: Why did GPT-2 find legal sentences more predictable than everyday ones?
options: GPT-2 was fine-tuned on contracts before it was released.
Legal boilerplate is templated and repeated across the web, so GPT-2 saw a lot of it.
Legal sentences are shorter, and perplexity always falls on shorter text.
The everyday sentences had spelling mistakes in them that raised their perplexity a lot.
questions.explanation: Phrases like "notwithstanding the foregoing" are low-entropy and appear in contracts, terms of service and licences all over the web. Nothing in the chapter says GPT-2 was fine-tuned on contracts or that the general sentences were misspelled.

questions.prompt: A hospital assumes its clinical notes need CPT because medicine "is a specialised domain". What does the chapter advise?
options: Skip CPT. Medicine is always well covered, as the legal example proved.
Start CPT at once. Medical text is always far from web data.
Run the perplexity gap test first. Domains that feel specialised can be well covered on the web.
Use IFT instead. CPT can't learn medical vocabulary.
questions.explanation: The worked example's lesson is that intuition about which domains are hard isn't reliable. Measure first. The legal result doesn't prove medicine is covered either. Clinical notes may have unusual phrasing, which only a test will show.

bookExercises.prompt: State the three-way distinction between CPT, IFT, and RAG in one sentence each, using the "what it changes" framing from Motivation.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: CPT changes what the model knows (self-supervised next-token prediction on domain text, no behaviour change). IFT changes how the model behaves (supervised training on instruction-response pairs, communication style not knowledge). RAG changes what the model can look up (external retrieval at inference time, weights never change).

bookExercises.prompt: Write the FLOPs formula $C \approx 6ND$ and state what each of the two terms represents.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `C ≈ 6 · N · D`: `N` is the model's parameter count, `D` is the number of training tokens processed. The `6` combines roughly 2 FLOPs/parameter/token for the forward pass and roughly 4 for the backward pass (backward does about twice the work of forward).

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 33.4's measured result (gap ratio 0.84x, legal text scoring *lower* perplexity than general text), explain what decision Procedure 33.1's own thresholds would recommend here, and why this result would have surprised someone who assumed "legal language is specialised, so it must have high perplexity."
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Procedure 33.1's own thresholds classify a ratio below 1.2 as "base model handles the domain well enough, try prompting/IFT first," and the measured 0.84x falls well under that threshold, so the test recommends against CPT entirely (and the direction is even more extreme than "well enough," since legal text was actually easier for the model than general text). This would surprise someone who assumed legal language's superficial unfamiliarity (Latin phrases, unusual syntax) implies statistical unpredictability to a language model. But the underlying reason is that highly templated, formulaic legal boilerplate is common across the public web (contracts, ToS pages) and therefore well-represented in GPT-2's pretraining data, even though it *reads* as specialised to a human.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 33.5's measured memory figures (full fine-tune 1.99GB vs. LoRA 0.27GB for GPT-2 small), compute the actual memory reduction factor, and explain why this is larger than the "3-4x" figure Exposition cites as typical for bigger models.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `1.99 / 0.27 ≈ 7.4x` memory reduction. This is larger than the "3-4x" figure Exposition cites for bigger models because LoRA's memory cost has two components: the frozen base model (2 bytes/param, fixed regardless of scale) and the trainable adapters (16 bytes/param × a small fraction of N). At small scale, the frozen-base term is tiny in absolute terms, so LoRA's total memory is dominated almost entirely by the adapter term, which is a very small fraction of the full 16-bytes/param figure. That produces a larger relative reduction than at bigger scale, where the frozen base term itself becomes large enough to matter more in the LoRA-vs-full comparison.

bookExercises.prompt: A team assumes their internal engineering wiki (full of unusual internal jargon and acronyms) definitely needs CPT without testing first. Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what they should do before committing budget.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Before committing CPT budget, run Procedure 33.1's domain gap test directly against your engineering wiki text versus general text. This chapter's Worked Example showed that a domain that feels highly specialised (legal contract language) can actually score *lower* perplexity than everyday sentences, because formulaic or repetitive text is often well-represented in a model's pretraining data regardless of how unfamiliar it looks to a person. 'Feels specialised' and 'is statistically unfamiliar to the model' are different claims, and only the second one justifies CPT."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 33.3's curation pipeline runs deduplication before quality filtering. Explain what could go wrong, in terms of wasted compute, if the order were reversed: quality filtering first, deduplication last.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Running quality filtering before deduplication means every duplicate copy of a document gets filtered (language ID, length, perplexity, domain classification) redundantly. If a document appears 50 times in the raw corpus, quality filtering runs 50 separate times on functionally identical text, wasting that much compute on redundant filtering work before deduplication ever removes the duplicates. Running deduplication first means the 50 copies collapse to one before any filtering compute is spent, so filtering only ever processes each unique document once.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about the "DoReMi" domain-reweighting approach (Xie et al., 2023) referenced in this chapter's Further Reading. Explain in your own words how it differs from picking a single fixed domain-mixing ratio (like the 80-90% figure in Exposition) by hand.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Manually picking a single fixed domain-mixing ratio (e.g. 85% domain / 15% general) applies the same static blend throughout training regardless of how the model's performance on each type of data evolves. DoReMi instead learns the mixing ratios by training a small proxy model to find domain weights that minimize worst-case loss across domains, then applies those learned weights to the larger training run. It treats the mixture ratio itself as something to be optimized empirically per-domain-set rather than fixed by an intuition-based percentage, which can better balance domains with very different intrinsic difficulty or size than a single hand-picked ratio would.
